before.stem: Regarding the accessory nerve, which of the following statements is INCORRECT:
options: The nerve originates from cervical segments C1 - C5. & The nerve exits the skull through the jugular foramen. 6%
The accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscle. (\/) Accessory nerve palsy results in the inability to nod the head. 66%
The nerve enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: Accessory nerve palsy results in inability to shrug the shoulders and to rotate the head to look at the opposite side to the lesion. Vv

after.stem: Regarding the accessory nerve, which of the following statements is INCORRECT:
options: The nerve originates from cervical segments C1–C5.
The nerve exits the skull through the jugular foramen.
The accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscle.
Accessory nerve palsy results in the inability to nod the head.
The nerve enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Accessory nerve palsy impairs shoulder shrugging and rotation of the head, not nodding. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and exits via the jugular foramen.
after.learningNote: Accessory nerve palsy impairs shoulder shrugging and rotation of the head, not nodding. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and exits via the jugular foramen.
after.highYieldNote: Accessory nerve palsy impairs shoulder shrugging and rotation of the head, not nodding. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and exits via the jugular foramen.
after.mnemonic: XI shrugs and turns: trapezius and SCM; nodding is not its main deficit.

before.stem: A patient presents with an adducted eye at rest which cannot abduct past the midline, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: Abducens nerve palsies result in a convergent squint at rest (eye turned inwards) with inability to abduct the eye because of unopposed action of the rectus medialis. The patient complains of horizontal diplopia when looking towards the affected side. With complete paralysis, the eye cannot abduct past the midline. Vv

after.stem: A patient presents with an adducted eye at rest which cannot abduct past the midline, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Abducens palsy causes an adducted, convergent eye because the lateral rectus cannot abduct the eye; severe palsy prevents abduction beyond the midline.
after.learningNote: Abducens palsy causes an adducted, convergent eye because the lateral rectus cannot abduct the eye; severe palsy prevents abduction beyond the midline.
after.highYieldNote: Abducens palsy causes an adducted, convergent eye because the lateral rectus cannot abduct the eye; severe palsy prevents abduction beyond the midline.
after.mnemonic: VI abducts; without it, medial rectus pulls the eye inward.

before.stem: w A 50 year old man presents to ED with diplopia and a ptosis. On pulling his eyelid up, you note that his pupil is looking down and out, and his pupil is fixed and dilated. Further imaging shows that the patient has a cerebral aneurysm compressing a cranial nerve. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely to be the culprit:
options: Middle cerebral artery & Posterior cerebral artery 9%
before.explanation: Ptosis, fixed dilated pupil and eye resting in down and out position are clinical features of a oculomotor (CN III) palsy. The cisternal portion of the oculomotor nerve is in the subarachnoid space anterior to the midbrain and in close proximity to the posterior communicating artery. Posterior communicating artery aneurysm is an important cause of oculomotor palsy. } Vv

warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.

before.stem: Regarding the trochlear nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: The trochlear nerve has both sensory and motor function. 2%
The trochlear nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle. 4%
The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve palsy results in loss of eyeball adduction. 4%
before.explanation: The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. It has the longest intracranial course. It is a purely motor nerve, which innervates the superior oblique muscle responsible for intorsion, depression and abduction of the eye. Vv

after.stem: Regarding the trochlear nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: The trochlear nerve has both sensory and motor function.
The trochlear nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle.
The trochlear nerve has the shortest intracranial course.
The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve palsy results in loss of eyeball adduction.
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: The trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
after.learningNote: The trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
after.highYieldNote: The trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
after.mnemonic: CN IV enters through SOF and supplies SO: superior oblique.

before.stem: A 55 year old woman presents to ED complaining of vertical diplopia with difficulty walking downstairs. She is tilting her head to one side as she says this helps ease the diplopia. Which of the following extraocular muscles is responsible for this picture:
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The superior oblique, innervated by the trochlear nerve, acts to cause intorsion, depression and abduction of the eyeball. In trochlear nerve palsy the patient complains of difficulty reading or walking downstairs and of vertical diplopia. The eye is extorted and may be elevated and the patient may head tilt to the opposite side of the palsy to compensate. Cc | Se Teer Vv

before.stem: Ww A patient presents with spontaneous onset of left sided facial weakness but is otherwise well. He is unable to purse his lips, close his eye fully or raise his eyebrow on the left side, which of the following is the most likely cause:
before.explanation: The most common cause of isolated lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy is Bell's palsy. If the damage is peripheral (LMN), the forehead will be involved and there will be an inability to close the eyes or raise the eyebrows. If the damage is central (UMN) there is forehead sparing as the frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles are innervated bilaterally. Vv

after.stem: A patient presents with spontaneous onset of left sided facial weakness but is otherwise well. He is unable to purse his lips, close his eye fully or raise his eyebrow on the left side, which of the following is the most likely cause:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: An isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, eyelid closure, and lower face is most commonly Bell's palsy when the patient is otherwise well.
after.learningNote: An isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, eyelid closure, and lower face is most commonly Bell's palsy when the patient is otherwise well.
after.highYieldNote: An isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, eyelid closure, and lower face is most commonly Bell's palsy when the patient is otherwise well.
after.mnemonic: Bell’s palsy affects the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead.

memoryAid.coreFact: An isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, eyelid closure, and lower face is most commonly Bell's palsy when the patient is otherwise well.
